THEODOSIUS
OF TRIPOLI
THREE BOOKS ON SPHERES.

PREFACE.

It is not certain among writers whether Theodosius was a native of the city of Tripoli, which is described by geographers and historians as being in both Phoenicia and Africa. Nor do they agree on the time when he flourished; however, it is not a weak conjecture that he lived around the time of Pompey the Great, because Strabo writes that he flourished in Bithynia at the same time as Asclepiades the physician (who, if we believe Pliny, flourished during the time of Pompey the Great). He wrote various mathematical works, including *On Habitations*, *On Nights and Days*, and also these three books on Spheres, which are presented with great learning, in which he demonstrates various properties of the sphere, the knowledge of which is greatly necessary for understanding the doctrine of celestial things. Indeed, without them, astronomy cannot maintain its dignity in any way. The principles of gnomonics also, or the method of constructing sundials, depend greatly on them. Add that they are also of considerable importance for properly understanding geography and perspective, as for the time being we remain silent about other uses of the elements of spheres.

But since Aristotle admits that the heavens are animate and have a principle of motion because they have differences in position, a considerable difficulty arises for us; for if it were moved by an intrinsic principle, it would not need an external mover; and therefore, through those things that are moved, we cannot rightly inquire into the motive powers. Therefore, either the soul of the heavens is some substance separate from the body, remaining immobile while moving, and not being moved itself; or it is the very form that acts upon the celestial body, and by accident is moved with the motion of the heavens, if it were an immobile substance. Certainly, active power would not be in the celestial body, but would flow from an external principle. But if it were a form, even though it had a principle of motion within it, passive power would not be entirely excluded from it, for as an active power demonstrates itself to be predicted, while it receives motive power from the first mover through intelligences, and that power is strengthened by another power, its passive power is rather judged. Therefore, when it first moves by virtue delivered from the first mover into itself, it clearly appears that the first principle of motion is from another. And even more so, because the motion of the heavens becomes deficient and is open to every irregularity, it seems to originate from the first mover rather than from the soul. The power of the soul does not extend to this, to be able to move it deficiently and always in the same way; this is indeed the task of the first mover, who always moves in the same way, never fails, and perfects all things with his infinite power. But returning to our purpose, it seems very likely that the earth around the core and the firmament surrounding the center of the earth are not entirely of one nature, but of different composition. At the bottom of the sea, where it reaches the center, it is muddy; but in other parts of the earth, and in the mountains leaning against the firmament of the earth, through which the central water rises again and seeps out like vapor, it is porous. Then, since we have said that in the center of the earth this water is converted into vapor, I prefer to attribute this to the internal heat and activity of the waters, rather than to some unknown intelligence, or angel delegated to that task by some. Natural things always seem to me to be explained naturally, especially when obvious natural causes are at hand.

Furthermore, let no one think that our opinion, in which we state that the central water is carried upwards as vapor and resolved into springs, is new and absurd; we will cite the agreement of various physicists, such as Fromond, Cabe, Moor, and Descartes. The former explicitly stipulates this to us when he says: "A mountain is like the head of an alembic in the distillations of chemists, in which vapors expelled upwards by a slow heat are cooled, and return to their natural density both by the internal form of the water and by the cold of the surrounding rocks: first drop by drop, but then many flowing together like rain into a single stream, gathering growth with a longer circuit, and finally bubbling forth from a full vein." From this it is clear that the generation of springs is plainly akin to rain, and so on. I do not mean to bring forward these and many other testimonies; but we will turn to the testimony of Holy Scripture, for this is how the Scriptural text reads: "For the Lord God had not yet made rain, and there was no man to till the ground, but a spring came up from the earth, irrigating the whole surface of the earth, and so on." It should be noted that the original text places vapor for the word "spring"; then it adds that the whole surface of the earth was irrigated, namely, the central vapor having passed through all permeable parts.

Why was the earth first irrigated by the earth's subterranean vapor, and not by superterranean rain, and thus stimulated to its first fertility? We will explain this later, when we discuss the fertility of central vapor. However, in this place, if we consider why some versions of Holy Scripture place vapor, while others place spring, we can easily reconcile them; for vapors, when they cool, are resolved into waters and springs, as all chemical distillations testify. This happens in two ways: — sometimes someone speaks of themselves, not beyond what is in them, but beyond what people think of them; as the Apostle says in 2 Corinthians 12:6: *“I boast that I am not deficient in any respect.”* — In another way, someone vaunts themselves with words, speaking of themselves beyond what is actually in them according to the truth of the matter. Regarding the first point, it can be said that the reasoning proceeds from vaunting as it exceeds opinion.

We arrange these circles and spheres so that, at a certain time, those observing them are struck. Thus, even though ships may have full sails, they appear to stand still. Someone will demonstrate at some point in which parts the comets wander. Since they are so drawn away from the others, and of whatever kind they are. We are content with our discoveries, if they may contribute something to truth and to posterity. "Through the stars," he says, "we do not see the further reaches, we pass through the ranks of comets." First, if this happens, it does not happen in the part where the star itself is a dense and solid fire, but where a rare brilliance flashes out and scatters into the hair. You see through the intervals of the fires, not through the fires themselves. "The stars," he says, "are all round, comets are elongated, from which it appears that stars are not." But who will grant you that comets are long, whose nature is like that of other globes? Moreover, their brightness extends, just as the sun emits its rays far and wide. Moreover, their form is different, both the body and that which shines from it. Thus, the body of a comet itself becomes rounded. But the brightness appears longer than that of other stars. Why do you ask: "Tell me first, why does the moon receive light differently from the sun, when it receives it from the sun?" Why does it sometimes redden, sometimes pale? Why is it livid and dark when it is excluded from the sight of the sun? Tell me why all the stars have some difference in their appearance, differing greatly from the sun. How does nothing prevent the stars from being dissimilar, just as nothing prevents comets from being eternal and of the same kind as the others, even if they do not have a similar appearance? What then is the world itself, if you consider it, but composed of diverse things? What is it that in the sign of the Ram the sun always burns, and scorches the lands with heat? In the sign of the Water Bearer, it constricts winter? It freezes the rivers? And yet this and that sign originate from the same condition, though their nature is different in effect and character. Within the briefest time, the Ram is exalted, the Libra sinks very slowly, and yet this sign and that are of the same nature, as the one ascends in a short time, the other is prolonged for a long time. Do you not see that contrary elements are among themselves? There are heavy and light, cold and hot, moist and dry. The entire harmony of this world consists of discord. You deny that a comet is a star because its form does not conform to the pattern, nor is it similar to the others. You see that it is most similar to that which returns to its place in the thirtieth year, to this one which returned to its seat within a year. It does not perform its work according to a single form, but boasts of its variety. Some are more sluggish, others faster, some have produced [effects], others more temperate. Some it has led away from the crowd, so that each one might proceed distinctly and conspicuously, others it has sent into a group. He ignores the power of nature who does not think it can ever do anything but what it frequently does. Comets do not show themselves frequently, he attributes to them a different place, different times, dissimilar motions from the others. He wanted to magnify the magnitude of his work from these, whose more beautiful appearance is not to be thought of as chance, whether you consider their size or their brightness, which is greater and more intense than that of others. But it has a remarkable and singular appearance, not thrown together hastily and crafted, but freely released and embracing the region of many stars. Aristotle says that comets signify storms and the violence of winds and rains. So what? Do you not think it is a star that foretells the future? For it is not so like a sign of a storm, as how the sparkling of oil foretells future rain, and how the growth of fungi indicates the decay of things, or how the desertion of the shorebirds and the high cloud floating above indicate a furious sea. But so, as how the equinox turns to heat and cold of the year. And how those things which the Chaldeans sing, what a newly born star establishes as happy or sad. To know that this is so, the comet does not threaten winds and rains immediately upon its rising, as Aristotle says, but makes the whole year suspect. From this it appears that it is not drawn from the near, to give signs for the near, but has laws established and compressed by the laws of the world. This comet appeared when Patruculus and Vopiscus were consuls, which was predicted by Aristotle and Theophrastus. There were great and continuous storms everywhere. But in Achaia and Macedonia, cities were overturned by earth movements. He says, "The slowness of these is an argument that they are heavier, and contain much of the earth." Moreover, their courses are almost compelled towards the cardinal points. Both of these are false. I will speak of the first before the other, because those that are carried more slowly are heavy. So what? Is the star of Saturn, which completes its course most slowly of all, heavy? But it has an argument for lightness, because it is above the others. But you say, it traverses a larger orbit.
